questions.question: What exactly was announced, signed, published and made effective between 2 and 10 April, and on what dates?
questions.answer: Order signed 2 April, published 7 April; 10 per cent from 5 April, Annex I rates from 9 April, suspended from 10 April for all partners but China. Still needed: the announcement wording on 2 April.

questions.question: Which legal authorities did the administration use for each tariff programme, and what aims did it state?
questions.answer: Not yet researched.

questions.question: How were tariffs used for non-trade aims (drugs, migration, deportation flights, political disputes)?
questions.answer: Not yet researched.

questions.question: What did the February orders on Canada and Mexico require, when did they take effect, and what was exempted?
questions.answer: Not yet researched.

questions.question: How did Canada and Mexico respond, and with what measures and values?
questions.answer: Canada retaliated in stages (C$30 billion from 4 March, C$29.8 billion from 13 March, autos from 9 April) and lifted most counter-tariffs on 1 September; Mexico did not retaliate, instead trading a 10,000-strong National Guard deployment for a pause (3 February), winning a USMCA exemption (6 March) and a 90-day standstill (31 July).

questions.question: How did markets move between 2 and 9 April, and what did the administration cite when it paused?
questions.answer: Official data: the 10-year yield rose 47 bp between 4 and 11 April; Fed staff describe a sharp deterioration reversed after the pause. The pause order cites more than 75 partners seeking talks. Still needed: exchange-sourced daily index changes (AP, Reuters and FRED were not reachable on 21 October 2026).

questions.question: What did the 9 April order and the 11 April electronics exemption change?
questions.answer: EO 14266 suspended country rates for 90 days from 10 April (10 per cent for all but China) and raised China to 125 per cent; the 11 April memorandum exempted computers, smartphones and semiconductors retroactive to 5 April.

questions.question: What were the successive US rates on Chinese goods, by instrument and effective date?
questions.answer: Fentanyl duty 10 per cent from 4 February (EO 14195), 20 per cent from 4 March (EO 14228), back to 10 per cent from 10 November (EO 14357). Reciprocal 34 per cent from 9 April, 84 (EO 14259), 125 per cent from 10 April (EO 14266): total additional 145 per cent; reduced at Geneva to 10 per cent reciprocal from 14 May. Still needed: the Geneva implementing order and the August and November extensions.

questions.question: What countermeasures did China take (tariffs, export controls, entity lists, purchases)?
questions.answer: China retaliated by tranche: energy and machinery (10 February), farm goods (10 March), 34 per cent on all US goods (10 April) rising to 84 and 125 per cent, rare-earth export licensing from 4 April, and broader October controls later suspended (7 November) to 10 November 2026.

questions.question: What did the Geneva, Stockholm and Busan arrangements actually commit each side to?
questions.answer: Geneva implemented by both sides on 14 May; Busan arrangement per US fact sheet and Chinese announcement No. 70. Still needed: Stockholm extension texts and the US order implementing the November reciprocal suspension.

questions.question: What did the deals with the UK, Japan, the EU, South Korea, Indonesia, the Philippines and Vietnam commit?
questions.answer: EU (21 August framework), Japan (EO 14345, 15 per cent all-in, $550 billion), Korea (13 November fact sheet, 15 per cent, $350 billion in two parts) recorded from primary texts. Still needed: UK (8 May), Vietnam, Indonesia and Philippines texts.

questions.question: What rates took effect on 7 August, and why were Brazil, India and Canada singled out for higher rates?
questions.answer: New rates from 7 August (EO 14326); Canada 35 per cent from 1 August (EO 14325); Brazil +40 per cent from 6 August for political reasons including the Bolsonaro prosecution (EO 14323), eased for farm goods from 13 November (EO 14361); India +25 per cent from 27 August for Russian oil (EO 14329).

questions.question: How were Section 232 sector tariffs (steel, aluminium, autos, copper and others) expanded during the year?
questions.answer: Section 232: steel and aluminium 25 per cent for all from 12 March, 50 per cent from 4 June; autos 25 per cent from 3 April (parts by 3 May); copper semi-finished 50 per cent from 1 August; timber 10 and furniture and cabinets 25 per cent from 14 October; trucks 25 and buses 10 per cent from 1 November.

questions.question: How did the courts rule on the emergency-powers tariffs, from the Court of International Trade to the Supreme Court?
questions.answer: CIT (28 May 2025) held all IEEPA tariff orders unlawful and enjoined them; the Federal Circuit stayed that on 10 June, then affirmed 7-4 on 29 August while vacating the universal injunction; the Supreme Court affirmed 6-3 on 20 February 2026 that IEEPA authorizes no tariffs. The tariffs were collected throughout 2025. Refunds and replacement measures fall after the chapter's year and belong in the epilogue note.

questions.question: What did Congress do: votes on resolutions and any legislation?
questions.answer: Senate passed S.J.Res. 37 on 2 April, 51-48. Still needed: House action, the House rule blocking expedited votes, and later Senate votes on other emergencies.

questions.question: Which trade agreements not involving the United States were concluded in 2025?
questions.answer: Primary records for EFTA-Mercosur (16 September), EU-Indonesia (23 September), China-ASEAN 3.0 (28 October), UK-India (24 July) and Mexico's duties on non-agreement countries (from 1 January 2026). Still needed: India-New Zealand (December) and EU-Mercosur status.

questions.question: How did China's trade surplus reach US$1 trillion, and where did its exports go?
questions.answer: Surplus $1,188.98 billion (GACC, USD) or 8,509.4 billion yuan (NBS); exports to the US down 19.5 per cent, to ASEAN up 14.0 and the EU up 9.0 per cent.

questions.question: How much did US customs duties raise in 2025 compared with 2024?
questions.answer: Net customs receipts about $264.0 billion in calendar 2025 against $78.9 billion in 2024 (Treasury MTS Table 4); fiscal 2025 $194.9 billion against $77.0 billion.

questions.question: What was the average effective US tariff rate by year end, and how do estimates differ?
questions.answer: Statutory average about 16.8 per cent in November 2025 (Budget Lab). Still needed: an observed-duties rate from official data (customs receipts over imports) and a second independent estimate.

questions.question: What did tariffs do to prices, and who bore the cost? Where do estimates disagree?
questions.answer: Retrospective consumer-price effect 0.5-1.0 per cent per Budget Lab summary of later studies. Still needed: the underlying studies themselves (Tier 4 primary), import-price index evidence on incidence.

questions.question: What happened to the US goods trade deficit over 2025?
questions.answer: Goods deficit rose 2.1 per cent to a record $1,240.9 billion (first estimate; revised up about 1.5 per cent in June 2026); the deficit with China fell by $93.4 billion while deficits with Taiwan and Vietnam rose by $73.0 and $54.7 billion. The stated aim of shrinking the deficit was not met in 2025.

findings.finding: Executive Order 14257 is dated 2 April 2025 and was published in the Federal Register on 7 April 2025.

The 10 per cent baseline applied to goods entered on or after 12:01 a.m. EDT on 5 April 2025; country-specific Annex I rates from 12:01 a.m. EDT on 9 April 2025; goods already in transit on the final mode of transport were exempt.
The order invokes IEEPA, the National Emergencies Act, section 604 of the Trade Act of 1974 and 3 U.S.C. 301, and declares a national emergency based on large and persistent goods trade deficits.
findings.quotation: I hereby declare a national emergency with respect to this threat.

findings.finding: The order states the goods trade deficit had grown by over 40 per cent in five years, reaching $1.2 trillion in 2024.

Annex I lists 57 trading partners with country rates from 11 to 50 per cent, including China 34, the EU 20, Japan 24, South Korea 25, India 26, Taiwan 32, Switzerland 31, Vietnam 46, Cambodia 49 and Lesotho 50 per cent. The United Kingdom does not appear (baseline 10 per cent only).

Exempt from the reciprocal duties: 50 U.S.C. 1702(b) articles, steel, aluminium and autos already under Section 232, Annex II products (including copper, pharmaceuticals, semiconductors, lumber, certain critical minerals, energy), Column 2 countries, and goods subject to future Section 232 actions.
By 2 April, USMCA-qualifying goods of Canada and Mexico remained exempt; non-qualifying goods were subject to 25 per cent, with Canadian energy, energy resources and potash at 10 per cent.

The order reserves power to raise duties if a partner retaliates and to lower them if a partner remedies non-reciprocal arrangements and aligns with the United States on economic and national security matters.

Executive Order 14193 (signed 1 February 2025) imposed an additional 25 per cent duty on products of Canada and 10 per cent on Canadian energy and energy resources, effective 12:01 a.m. ET on 4 February 2025, under IEEPA.
The Canada order rests on a declared emergency over the flow of illicit drugs across the northern border, and reserves the right to increase duties if Canada retaliates.
findings.quotation: Should Canada retaliate against the United States in response to this action through import duties

findings.finding: Duty-free de minimis treatment was withdrawn for goods covered by the Canada order.

Executive Order 14194 (1 February 2025) imposed an additional 25 per cent duty on products of Mexico, effective 12:01 a.m. ET on 4 February 2025, citing an emergency over illicit drugs and illegal migration.
Executive Order 14195 (1 February 2025) imposed an additional 10 per cent duty on products of China, effective 12:01 a.m. ET on 4 February 2025, citing the synthetic-opioid supply chain.

Executive Order 14259 (8 April 2025) raised the reciprocal rate on China from 34 to 84 per cent from 12:01 a.m. EDT on 9 April, citing China's 4 April announcement of a 34 per cent counter-tariff effective 10 April.
Executive Order 14266 (9 April 2025) raised the reciprocal rate on China from 84 to 125 per cent from 12:01 a.m. EDT on 10 April, citing China's 84 per cent counter-tariff announced 9 April.
The same order suspended the higher Annex I country rates for 90 days, from 10 April until 12:01 a.m. EDT on 9 July 2025, leaving a 10 per cent rate for all Annex I partners except China.
The US order records that on 4 April 2025 China's State Council Tariff Commission announced a 34 per cent tariff on all US goods, effective 10 April.
Duties on low-value postal shipments from China were raised from 30 to 90 per cent (8 April) and then to 120 per cent (9 April), with per-item alternatives raised as well.

The Supreme Court decided Learning Resources v. Trump, with V.O.S. Selections, on 20 February 2026 (argued 5 November 2025), holding that IEEPA does not authorize the President to impose tariffs; both the drug-trafficking tariffs on Canada, Mexico and China and the reciprocal tariffs were challenged.
findings.quotation: IEEPA does not authorize the President to impose tariffs.

findings.finding: The Federal Circuit judgment (149 F. 4th 1312, en banc) was affirmed; the D.C. district court case was vacated and remanded for lack of jurisdiction.

Chief Justice Roberts wrote for the Court in Parts I, II-A-1 and II-B, joined by Justices Sotomayor, Kagan, Gorsuch, Barrett and Jackson; Parts II-A-2 and III (major questions) were joined only by Gorsuch and Barrett. Justices Thomas, Alito and Kavanaugh dissented.
The Court of International Trade had granted summary judgment to five small businesses and 12 States; the Federal Circuit en banc held the tariffs unbounded in scope, amount and duration.
findings.quotation: are unbounded in scope, amount, and duration

findings.finding: In the joint statement of 12 May 2025 from Geneva, the United States agreed, by 14 May 2025, to suspend 24 percentage points of the reciprocal rate on China for an initial 90 days, keeping 10 per cent, and to remove the increases made by Executive Orders 14259 and 14266.
findings.quotation: suspending 24 percentage points of that rate for an initial period of 90 days

findings.finding: China agreed to mirror the suspension on its counter-tariff, remove the later increases (Tariff Commission announcements No. 5 and 6 of 2025), and suspend or remove non-tariff countermeasures taken since 2 April 2025.
Talks were to continue between Vice Premier He Lifeng and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent with Trade Representative Jamieson Greer.

By the US account of 1 November 2025, China agreed to suspend the rare-earth export controls announced on 9 October 2025, issue general licences for rare earths, gallium, germanium, antimony and graphite, suspend retaliatory tariffs and countermeasures taken since 4 March 2025, and buy at least 12 million tonnes of US soybeans in the last two months of 2025 and 25 million tonnes a year in 2026-2028.

The United States agreed to cut the fentanyl-related tariff by 10 percentage points from 10 November 2025, keep the higher reciprocal rate on China suspended until 10 November 2026, and suspend for a year the affiliates export-control rule and the Section 301 shipbuilding measures.
Executive Order 14228 (3 March 2025) raised the fentanyl-related duty on Chinese goods from 10 to 20 per cent.
Executive Order 14357 (4 November 2025) cut the fentanyl-related duty on Chinese goods from 20 to 10 per cent effective 10 November 2025, citing Chinese commitments on precursor chemicals.

Arithmetic check: from 10 April the additional duty on most Chinese goods was 125 per cent (reciprocal) plus 20 per cent (fentanyl) = 145 per cent. The archive entry of 9 April that reports a rise to 125 per cent "up from 104" mixes a reciprocal-only figure with a total and needs correction in the text.

On 28 May 2025 a three-judge panel of the Court of International Trade granted summary judgment to five small businesses and 12 States, holding that IEEPA authorizes none of the worldwide, retaliatory or trafficking tariff orders, and vacated and permanently enjoined them.
findings.quotation: IEEPA does not authorize any of the Worldwide, Retaliatory, or Trafficking Tariff Orders.

findings.finding: On 10 June 2025 the Federal Circuit granted a stay pending appeal and ordered en banc hearing, with argument on 31 July 2025; the tariffs therefore stayed in force while the case was appealed.
findings.quotation: The motions for a stay pending appeal are granted.

findings.locator: Per curiam, p. 4-5 and Part VI, p. 44-45
findings.finding: On 29 August 2025 the en banc Federal Circuit, 7-4, affirmed that the trafficking and reciprocal tariffs exceeded IEEPA, but vacated the universal injunction and remanded on remedy; Judge Taranto dissented with Chief Judge Moore and Judges Prost and Chen.

Executive Order 14326 (31 July 2025) replaced the suspended April rates with new country rates effective 12:01 a.m. EDT seven days after the order, that is 7 August 2025, with goods in transit protected until 5 October. Unlisted partners stayed at 10 per cent.

New reciprocal rates included Switzerland 39, Syria 41, Laos and Myanmar 40, Iraq and Serbia 35, India 25, Taiwan and Vietnam 20, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Thailand, Cambodia and Pakistan 19, Japan and South Korea 15, the United Kingdom and Brazil 10 per cent.

For EU goods the order set a 15 per cent all-in ceiling: goods with an ordinary (Column 1) duty under 15 per cent were topped up to 15 per cent; goods already at or above 15 per cent paid no reciprocal duty.
Goods found to be transshipped to evade the duties were made subject to a 40 per cent rate plus penalties, with no mitigation.

Executive Order 14325 (31 July 2025) raised the duty on non-USMCA Canadian goods from 25 to 35 per cent from 12:01 a.m. EDT on 1 August 2025, citing Canada's retaliation; transshipped goods faced 40 per cent.

findings.locator: Comparison with archive entry of 1 August 2025
findings.finding: The archive entry stating that tariffs on more than 90 countries entered force on 1 August conflicts with the order, which set 7 August; only the Canadian increase began on 1 August. The book should follow the order.
Executive Order 14231 of 6 March 2025 exempted USMCA-qualifying Canadian goods and cut the duty on potash from 25 to 10 per cent.

Executive Order 14324 (30 July 2025) ended duty-free de minimis treatment for low-value shipments from all countries from 12:01 a.m. EDT on 29 August 2025, with temporary flat postal duties of $80, $160 or $200 per item depending on the origin country's IEEPA rate.

Executive Order 14329 (6 August 2025) added a further 25 per cent duty on Indian goods because India was 'directly or indirectly importing Russian Federation oil', effective 12:01 a.m. EDT 21 days later (27 August 2025). With the 25 per cent reciprocal rate this made 50 per cent.
findings.quotation: is currently directly or indirectly importing Russian Federation oil

findings.finding: In the first full-year estimate, the US goods and services deficit for 2025 was $901.5 billion, down $2.1 billion (0.2 per cent) from 2024; the goods deficit rose $25.5 billion (2.1 per cent) to $1,240.9 billion while the services surplus rose to $339.5 billion.

The goods deficit with China fell $93.4 billion to $202.1 billion (imports down $130.4 billion), while the deficits with Taiwan (up $73.0 billion to $146.8 billion) and Vietnam (up $54.7 billion to $178.2 billion) rose.

The June 2026 annual revision raised the 2025 goods and services deficit by 2.2 per cent, with a 1.5 per cent upward revision to the goods deficit; final figures should be taken from the revised tables.

findings.locator: Customs Duties, monthly net receipts, Jan 2024-Dec 2025
findings.finding: Net customs duties totalled about $264.0 billion in calendar 2025, against $78.9 billion in 2024. Monthly receipts rose from about $7-8 billion in January-March 2025 to $15.6 billion in April and about $30 billion a month from August.

findings.locator: Customs Duties, fiscal year to date, September 2025 and 2024
findings.finding: In fiscal year 2025 (October 2024-September 2025) net customs duties were $194.9 billion, against $77.0 billion in fiscal 2024.

The Budget Lab estimated in November 2025 that consumers faced an average effective tariff rate of 16.8 per cent, the highest since 1935 (14.4 per cent after substitution), with the price level raised 1.2 per cent in the short run; without the IEEPA tariffs the rate would be 9.3 per cent.
findings.quotation: the highest since 1935

findings.finding: A year on, the Budget Lab reported that retrospective estimates put the consumer-price effect of 2025 tariffs at 0.5-1.0 per cent, against its own April 2025 estimate of 2.3 per cent; the gap partly reflects rates that changed or were never enacted, and possibly incomplete pass-through or costs borne as lower incomes.
On 2 April 2025 the Senate passed S.J.Res. 37, terminating the Canada emergency, 51-48, with Republicans Collins, McConnell, Murkowski and Paul voting yes.

Canada announced 25 per cent counter-tariffs on C$155 billion of US goods: a first phase of C$30 billion (orange juice, peanut butter, wine, spirits, beer, appliances, apparel and others) and a further C$125 billion after a 21-day consultation.
Canadian counter-tariffs took effect on C$30 billion of US goods on 4 March 2025, on C$29.8 billion of steel, aluminium and other goods on 13 March, and on US vehicles on 9 April.

From 1 September 2025 Canada removed most of its March counter-tariffs, keeping those on steel, aluminium and automobiles, on the ground that most Canadian goods entered the United States tariff-free under CUSMA.
findings.quotation: Canada is removing counter tariffs put in place in March 2025 on most U.S. imports, effective September 1, 2025.

findings.finding: On 3 February 2025 Mexico secured a one-month pause of the 25 per cent tariffs by agreeing to reinforce the northern border with 10,000 National Guard troops against drug and especially fentanyl smuggling; the United States agreed to work against arms trafficking into Mexico, and working groups on security and trade were set up. Mexico announced no counter-tariffs.
findings.quotation: reforzar la frontera norte con 10 mil elementos de la Guardia Nacional

findings.finding: On 6 March 2025 President Sheinbaum announced that goods within the USMCA (T-MEC) would pay no tariff, until 2 April.
findings.quotation: no se le requerirá pagar aranceles en los productos que se encuentren dentro del Tratado

findings.finding: On 31 July 2025, after a call with President Trump, Mexico announced a 90-day standstill: no further increases, USMCA goods still exempt, and existing tariffs on autos, steel and aluminium maintained.
findings.quotation: Nos mantenemos como estamos y son 90 días

findings.locator: Decree and transitional articles, DOF 29 December 2025
findings.finding: Mexico enacted higher import duties, mostly 25-35 per cent and up to 50 per cent (passenger cars), on goods from countries without a trade agreement, effective 1 January 2026; at least 1,290 tariff lines were parsed from the decree. Commentary that most affected imports come from China is not yet from a primary source.

Executive Order 14323 (30 July 2025) imposed an additional 40 per cent on Brazilian goods from 12:01 a.m. EDT seven days later (6 August 2025), citing Brazilian orders compelling US platforms to censor content, actions of Justice Alexandre de Moraes, and the prosecution of former President Jair Bolsonaro; aircraft, energy, fertilizers, pulp and some metals were exempt.
findings.quotation: Brazilian officials are also persecuting former President of Brazil Jair Bolsonaro.

findings.finding: Executive Order 14361 (20 November 2025) exempted certain Brazilian agricultural products from the 40 per cent duty from 13 November 2025, citing initial progress in negotiations that followed a call between the presidents on 6 October.

China answered the first US tariff with additional duties from 10 February 2025: 15 per cent on US coal and liquefied natural gas, and 10 per cent on crude oil, agricultural machinery, large-engine cars and pickups.

After the US increase to 20 per cent, China imposed from 10 March 2025 additional duties of 15 per cent on US chicken, wheat, corn and cotton and 10 per cent on sorghum, soybeans, pork, beef, aquatic products, fruit, vegetables and dairy.
China raised its additional tariff on all US goods from 34 to 84 per cent from 12:01 p.m. on 10 April 2025.
China raised its additional tariff from 84 to 125 per cent from 12 April 2025 and said further US increases would serve no economic purpose.
findings.quotation: Even if the United States continues to raise tariffs, such action would serve no economic purpose

findings.finding: Implementing Geneva, China cut its additional tariff to 10 per cent from 12:01 p.m. on 14 May 2025, suspending 24 points for 90 days, and ceased the April increases.

On 4 April 2025, the day of its first counter-tariff on the reciprocal tariffs, China imposed export licensing, effective immediately, on seven medium and heavy rare earths: samarium, gadolinium, terbium, dysprosium, lutetium, scandium and yttrium.

On 7 November 2025 China suspended until 10 November 2026 the export-control announcements No. 55-58 and No. 61-62 of 2025, the October measures including controls on foreign-made rare-earth items and rare-earth technologies; the April controls (No. 18) were not among those suspended.

Proclamation 10896 (10 February 2025) restored a 25 per cent steel tariff on imports from all countries, ending prior exemptions, from 12:01 a.m. ET on 12 March 2025; aluminium was raised to 25 per cent by the companion Proclamation 10895.
Proclamation 10947 (3 June 2025) doubled the steel and aluminium tariffs from 25 to 50 per cent from 12:01 a.m. EDT on 4 June 2025.
Proclamation 10962 (30 July 2025) imposed 50 per cent on semi-finished copper products and intensive copper derivatives from 1 August 2025; refined copper was not tariffed.

Proclamation 10976 (29 September 2025) imposed 10 per cent on softwood timber and lumber and 25 per cent on certain upholstered wooden furniture, kitchen cabinets and vanities from 14 October 2025, capped at 10 per cent for the UK and at 15 per cent all-in for the EU and Japan.
Proclamation 10908 (26 March 2025) imposed 25 per cent on imported automobiles from 3 April 2025 and on parts by 3 May 2025, with USMCA vehicles taxed only on non-US content once certified.
Proclamation 10984 (17 October 2025) imposed 25 per cent on medium- and heavy-duty vehicles and key parts and 10 per cent on buses from 1 November 2025.

The EU-US framework of 21 August 2025 set a ceiling of the higher of MFN or 15 per cent on most EU goods, MFN-only treatment for aircraft, generic pharmaceuticals and unavailable natural resources from 1 September, and a 15 per cent auto rate conditional on EU legislation; the EU said it intended to remove tariffs on all US industrial goods, buy $750 billion of US energy through 2028 and $40 billion of AI chips, and expected $600 billion of European investment.

Executive Order 14345 (4 September 2025) implemented the Japan agreement: a 15 per cent all-in ceiling on most Japanese goods applied retroactively to 7 August 2025, sector treatment for autos and aircraft, and a stated Japanese commitment to invest $550 billion in projects selected by the US government.
findings.quotation: the Government of Japan has agreed to invest $550 billion in the United States

findings.locator: Fact sheet, trade and investment sections
findings.finding: The US-Korea joint fact sheet of 13 November 2025 (following the 29 October meeting in Gyeongju) set a 15 per cent rate on Korean goods and on autos and parts, with $150 billion of Korean shipbuilding investment and $200 billion under an investment memorandum, capped at $20 billion a year.
findings.quotation: the ROK shall not be required to fund an aggregate amount of U.S. dollars greater than $20 billion in any calendar year

findings.finding: The implementing notice made the Korean auto reduction effective for goods entered from 1 November 2025.

The memorandum of 11 April 2025 added computers (8471), smartphones (8517.13), semiconductors and related headings to the exceptions from the reciprocal tariffs, retroactive to 5 April, with refunds of duties already paid.
The 10-year Treasury yield fell from 4.20 per cent on 2 April to 4.01 on 4 April, then rose to 4.48 per cent by 11 April, a rise of 47 basis points in a week.

findings.locator: Staff review of the financial situation
findings.finding: Fed staff reported that tariff announcements caused a significant deterioration in global risk sentiment that largely reversed after the pause; Treasury market liquidity deteriorated after 2 April but the market continued to function; the trade-weighted dollar fell more than 2 per cent over the period.
findings.quotation: Tariff announcements led to a significant deterioration in global risk sentiment, which largely reversed following a subsequent pause

findings.finding: The pause order itself gave as its reason that more than 75 trading partners had approached the United States to negotiate rather than retaliate.
findings.quotation: more than 75 other foreign trading partners

findings.finding: China's customs data show 2025 exports of $3,771.9 billion (up 5.5 per cent), imports of $2,582.9 billion (flat) and a trade surplus of $1,188.98 billion.

China's statistical communiqué reports a 2025 goods surplus of 8,509.4 billion yuan (up 20.4 per cent), exports to the United States down 19.5 per cent, and exports to ASEAN up 14.0 per cent and to the EU up 9.0 per cent.
EFTA (Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway, Switzerland) and Mercosur (Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay, Uruguay) signed a free trade agreement in Rio de Janeiro on 16 September 2025.
findings.quotation: The FTA will create a free trade zone of almost 300 million people

findings.finding: The EU and Indonesia concluded negotiations on a Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement and an investment protection agreement on 23 September 2025.
findings.quotation: On 23 September 2025, the EU and Indonesia finalised negotiations for the CEPA and for an Investment Protection Agreement.

findings.finding: China and ASEAN signed the Free Trade Area 3.0 Upgrade Protocol in Kuala Lumpur on 28 October 2025, adding nine areas including the digital and green economies and supply-chain connectivity.
The UK and India signed a Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement on 24 July 2025 (in force 15 July 2026).
findings.quotation: The UK signed a trade deal with India on 24 July 2025 which entered into force on 15 July 2026.

findings.finding: The order found that a lack of reciprocity, disparate tariff rates, non-tariff barriers and partners' policies that suppress wages and consumption, as indicated by large and persistent goods deficits, constitute an unusual and extraordinary threat to the national security and economy of the United States.
findings.quotation: constitute an unusual and extraordinary threat to the national security and economy of the United States

findings.locator: Syllabus, p. 2 (opinion of the Court, Part II-A-1)
findings.finding: The Court recalled that Article I gives Congress the power to lay duties, and that the Government conceded the President has no inherent authority to impose tariffs in peacetime.
findings.quotation: The Government thus concedes that the President enjoys no inherent authority to impose tariffs during peacetime.

findings.locator: Syllabus, p. 3 (Part II-A-2, joined by Gorsuch and Barrett only)
findings.finding: The Chief Justice, for three Justices, noted that in IEEPA's half century no President had invoked it to impose any tariffs.
findings.quotation: in IEEPA's half century of existence, no President has invoked the statute to impose any tariffs

findings.finding: The steel proclamation cited the Commerce Secretary's view that the 2018 tariff of 25 per cent had worked, with steel capacity utilization rising above 80 per cent.
findings.quotation: the U.S. steel capacity utilization rate increased to above 80 percent

findings.finding: The Canada and Mexico orders were amended by orders of 3 February 2025 (Executive Orders 14197 and 14198, pausing them) and of early March (Executive Orders 14231 and 14227).

findings.locator: Developments in financial markets; staff review
findings.finding: The minutes record that equity prices declined sharply early in the intermeeting period before retracing, ending little changed, and that risky-asset prices were extremely volatile amid tariff developments.
findings.quotation: Prices of risky assets were extremely volatile over the intermeeting period amid multiple tariff-related developments.

findings.finding: Arithmetic: after Geneva the additional duty on most Chinese goods was 10 per cent (reciprocal) plus 20 per cent (fentanyl) = 30 per cent; after 10 November, 10 plus 10 = 20 per cent (S011).

The steel proclamation rests on section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962, under which the Commerce Secretary investigates whether imports threaten to impair national security and the President may adjust them.
findings.quotation: section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962

findings.finding: Executive Order 14197 (3 February 2025) paused the Canadian tariffs until 12:01 a.m. on 4 March 2025.
findings.quotation: paused and will not take effect until March 4, 2025, at 12:01 a

findings.finding: China's Announcement No. 61 of 9 October 2025 required licences for foreign-made items containing Chinese-origin rare-earth items worth 0.1 per cent or more of their value, and for items made abroad with Chinese rare-earth mining, separation, metallurgy, magnet or recycling technology; these parts were to apply from 1 December 2025.
findings.quotation: 价值比例达到0.1%及以上

findings.finding: The 31 July agreement followed a telephone conversation between President Sheinbaum and President Trump.
findings.quotation: en su conversación telefónica con el presidente de Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, se logró un buen acuerdo

findings.finding: In the April annex Switzerland was set at 31 per cent, Laos at 48 and Myanmar at 44.
The Mexico and China orders of 1 February also withdrew duty-free de minimis treatment for the goods they covered.
findings.quotation: duty-free de minimis treatment under 19 U.S.C. 1321 shall not be available

findings.finding: Proclamation 10895 of 10 February 2025 had raised the aluminium tariff to 25 per cent on imports from all countries.
